title: Lymphoedema after breast cancer: swelling, treatment and daily care
intro: Breast cancer treatment can disrupt lymph drainage, especially when lymph nodes or nearby tissue are affected by surgery or radiation. Fluid may then build up in an arm, hand, breast or chest area. This is called lymphoedema and can appear soon after treatment or years later. Early assessment can make management easier. Not every new swelling is lymphoedema, so unexplained changes should be checked rather than treated from an old diagnosis alone.

sections.heading: Notice heaviness and changes before swelling becomes obvious
paragraphs: An arm may feel heavy, tight or less flexible, or sleeves, rings and a watch may fit differently. Skin texture or the breast and chest area can also change. Describe when this began, whether it varies and how it affects dressing, work or sleep. Tell the team which cancer treatments you had and any recent injury or infection. Lymphoedema risk is not the same for every person, and developing it is not proof that you failed to follow advice. Do not wait until the difference is very large to ask for assessment.

sections.heading: Establish the cause and a useful baseline
paragraphs: The clinician examines the area and may measure limb size, volume or other features to guide treatment and review. Further tests depend on the findings and uncertainty. Infection, a blood clot and other causes of swelling may need consideration; a cancer history also matters in deciding what to investigate. Ask for referral to a lymphoedema professional and a plan that covers both the swollen area and your general health. A single home circumference measurement cannot establish the cause or determine which compression product is safe.

sections.heading: Use properly fitted compression and taught techniques
paragraphs: Treatment often combines compression, movement, skin care and specialist drainage techniques. An initial phase may reduce swelling, followed by ongoing measures to maintain control. A sleeve, glove, wrap or bandaging needs an individual fit and instructions; tighter is not automatically better. Report pain, tingling, cold fingers or colour change rather than accepting them as necessary. Ask how to put garments on, care for them and arrange review as size changes. Manual lymphatic drainage uses specific gentle techniques, not forceful massage, and should be taught or provided by a trained professional.

sections.heading: Keep moving and protect the skin with a realistic routine
paragraphs: A gradual, tailored activity plan can support function and fluid movement; avoiding all arm use can create other difficulties. Discuss strength work, work tasks and how to increase demands safely with the treating team. Clean and moisturise skin, address small wounds and protect against cuts or burns without becoming afraid of every normal activity. Tell healthcare staff about the swelling and treatment history and agree practical arrangements for procedures. Do not refuse necessary urgent care because of a general rule heard elsewhere. If garments or daily tasks are hard to manage, ask for aids or carer training.

sections.heading: Know urgent changes and the long-term goal
paragraphs: Rapidly increasing swelling, pain, warmth, spreading redness, fever or feeling unwell needs prompt assessment for infection or another cause. Severe breathlessness, chest pain, confusion or collapse requires emergency help. Do not try to massage away a hot, suddenly painful swollen arm or simply tighten compression while waiting. Follow your service's acute-illness instructions. Lymphoedema is usually a long-term condition: treatment aims to control swelling and improve comfort and function, not guarantee a cure. Selected specialist procedures may be considered, but ongoing care may still be needed. Review persistent problems, fit and emotional strain rather than struggling alone.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a tighter sleeve years later
examples.text: Years after breast cancer surgery, someone notices a heavy arm and tighter clothing. They contact their team and describe the change. After assessment, they receive a fitted plan rather than buying the strongest sleeve online or assuming treatment-related swelling needs no investigation.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: warmth and fever
examples.text: A person with established lymphoedema develops a hot painful area and fever. They seek prompt medical assessment and follow the acute-care advice instead of increasing massage or waiting for the next garment-fitting appointment.

questions: What is causing this swelling, and do I need other causes checked or specialist referral?
Which compression, exercises and drainage techniques fit my needs, and can you show me how to use them?
Which changes need urgent help, and how will we review long-term control and garment fit?
